newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin pulls Moscow strings from country home.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin pulls Moscow strings from country home.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, on an extended "working convalescence" outside Moscow, moved to restore unity among key defence planners on Friday and tentatively prepared a return to international travel.

Yeltsin, the vigour and colour of earlier days clearly faded, remained secluded at his country home through the day. For 40 minutes he met chief aide Anatoly Chubais while in Moscow his defence chiefs made a joint public appearance at his remote command to dispel reports of squabbling over reform.
"Rumours about what they describe as our rivalry are unfounded," Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said of his relations with Kremlin Defence Council secretary Yuri Baturin.
"We may express different views. But it is the commander-in- chief (Yeltsin) who issues final orders which we have to obey."
The event held a double significance.

Firstly it showed Yeltsin, despite his physical absence from the Kremlin for all but a few hours in recent weeks, publicly imposing his will on defence chiefs. Rodionov, however, offered little cheer to his superior.
Asked about Yeltsin's absences from work, he replied:
"I would really like to see our commander-in-chief back, healthy and capable of working as he has done in the past.
"Now I have to wait for better times. One is left to hope that contacts which existed between commander-in-chief and defence minister will soon be restored."
Rodionov said on Thursday night that the armed forces had decayed to a "horrifying state". He said if reforms were delayed, nuclear systems could be out of control in two years.

The second significance of the news conference was to show Yeltsin's involvement with defence policy as NATO prepares to extend eastwards -- a move both the president and his political opponents see as a direct threat to Russian security.

The 66-year-old president, who had heart surgery in November and developed pneumonia in January, is clearly eager to show he controls defence and foreign policy during diplomatic exchanges with the West over the NATO expansion.

He must be seen to extract from Western capitals some kind of formal acknowledgement of Russian interests before the alliance issues invitations to erstwhile Kremlin Warsaw Pact allies at a Madrid summit in July.

The image of a country drifting, rudderless, towards a foreign policy humiliation is something opponents would gladly promote. Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov will attempt to present a convincing strategy on NATO expansion at a closed-door session of the communist-dominated parliament on Friday.

Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, beaten by Yeltsin in July's presidential elections, called for a meeting of "the most influential political and state figures" to seek a way out of what he called a national crisis; a call was clearly intended to undermine Yeltsin's authority.
Yeltsin's health has stirred fears he might be unable to attend a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton provisionally scheduled for Washington in March.
The Kremlin said on Friday Yeltsin was weighing the possibility of changing the venue to Europe.
A Kremlin spokesman, in comments that clearly put the onus for any revision on Washington, said Yeltsin would listen to arguments put by Clinton before making any final decision.
No firm date has been set yet for the summit and Yeltsin's poor health would counsel caution against committing the Russian president to any foreign trips in the near future.
Parliament tackled the legacy of what must rank as the biggest strategic failure of Yeltsin's presidency -- the military campaign to crush rebel Chechnya.

Parliament passed a resolution approving in principle an amnesty for rebel leaders and clearing the way for ties between Moscow and Grozny. The resolution must now be endorsed in the detail where, as the Russian saying goes, the devil dwells.
